Follow the block at the top of the prompt you are answering; an earlier prompt's block no longer applies.

Its spec's Piton source, in ./spec, is only where edits to the spec go.

Read the spec from its compiled reference under .claude/reference, where inheritance, expressions, and links are already resolved, or, for one thing, from what `piton slice` prints for it with this harness's adapter.

Never read the .pi source under ./spec to learn what the spec says; that is only where edits to the spec go.

Before executing anything, read the spec it touches. Links to .claude/reference/... in the prompt are the spec for what they name. Read each one you need before changing anything it covers. Don't re-read something you've already read.
instructions:
We're only asking a question about the project. Answer it without changing anything.

When the work is about Suspense, its modes, its prompts, or its questions, or you are to write a prompt or a question for the user, first read .suspense/suspense-fluency.md once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Suspense works.

The code is located in ./src.

The spec's Piton source is in ./spec, which `piton slice` reads. Don't change it, and don't read it directly to learn what the spec says: read the compiled reference, or what `piton slice` prints, instead.

Whenever the user asks you for a prompt, or your answer suggests one for them to send, give each prompt as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-prompt` and the mode it is for, one of `code`, `chain`, `spec`, `ask`, or `freeform`, such as ```` ```suspense-prompt chain ````, holding only the prompt's text, ready to send, never as plain text, a quote, or any other code block, since only this form lets the user send it from your answer. Pick the mode that fits the work, `chain` when it changes both the spec and the code; the user can send it to Code, Chain, or Spec all the same. When you need the user to answer something before you can go on, write the question as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-question`, the question on its first lines and then, if there are answers to pick from, one per line, each starting with `- `. Use these blocks only for prompts and questions meant for the user, never for code or examples.

content.text:
This run can't be compared directly with #1, because the window was a different size. Run #1 was 2117×1018 and this one is 1756×507, which is only about 41% of the pixels. Some of the improvement comes from the smaller window, not the prepass.

| | #1 (no prepass, 2117×1018) | #2 (prepass, 1756×507) |
|---|---|---|
| Frame time without trees | 4.0 ms | 2.4 ms |
| Frame time with trees | 42.0 ms | 32.6 ms |
| Tree cost | 38.0 ms | 30.2 ms |
| Tree GPU time | 59 ms | 30 ms |
| 1% low cost | +88 ms | +60 ms |
| Active trees per frame | 2,434 | 2,362 |
| Worst frames | 128–418 ms | 279–332 ms |

**What it tells you anyway:**

1. **The trees' cost doesn't mostly scale with pixels.** The pixel count fell by almost 60% and the prepass was on, yet the tree cost only fell about 20%, from 38 ms to 30 ms. If foliage overdraw were the main problem, a smaller window alone would have cut much more. So much of the 30 ms is per-tree work rather than per-pixel work: vertex work from thousands of trees and sprites, shadow casting, and re-uploading the per-frame batches.
2. **The per-frame tree problem is unchanged.** About 2,360 trees are still re-selected every frame, as you'd expect, since the prepass doesn't touch that.
3. **The spikes are just as bad or worse.** All eight worst frames are now around 280–330 ms with no tree CPU work, so they look like GPU stalls. A smaller window didn't help, which again points away from pixel cost. Shader compiles or buffer uploads are the likely causes, but neither is confirmed.

This makes the first two items in the Code prompt from my last answer the priority: the 2,400 per-frame trees and the spikes. The prepass looks like a minor gain at best. That prompt still applies as written.

To measure the prepass on its own, run both at the same window size, with DevTools undocked or closed so the window doesn't shrink:
```
http://localhost:3000/games/rally/?map=jackie&quality=medium&treebench=trees
http://localhost:3000/games/rally/?map=jackie&quality=medium&treebench=trees&treeprepass=1
```
`treebench=trees` skips the run without trees, so each test takes half as long. To compare, look at `avgMs` and `treeGpuMs` in the trees run, since `treeCostMs` needs the run without trees.
